items.body:
Holy moly, this is fire! Released by Heat Crimes in collaboration with Thessaloniki's Elhellell label, ‘Paradise Metal’ introduces the fretless electric guitar devotionals of Father Dionysios Tabakis, a 52 year old priest from the historic Greek city of Nafplio, who voices Byzantine church songs in a mix of amp worship hymns and outernational trance movements akin to Sir Richard Bishop or Sandy Bull via László Hortobágyi at Christian Love Forum’s sunday skool. WTF gear of the highest calibre…

‘Paradise Metal’ is one of many reasons why we keep reiterating: Heat Crimes is one of the best labels out there right now. At more than one point did we have to pinch ourselves at the the holy father’s procession of epiphanies effortlessly bridging ancient, microtonal Byzantine modes with DIY electronic modernism, often in jaw-dropping juxtapositions; sublime new age ambient to shoe-gazy basslines and mountaintop guitar shreds to techno incantations. Honestly it’s floored us in so many ways and is bound to exert the same effect with any of you lot, especially if you’re on a mission to sniff out incredible music from unknown margins.

The dozen songs speak richly to Father Dionysios Tabakis’ life immersed in the Orthodox church, and namely the historic Church of Panagitsa in Nafplio (Nativity of the Theotokos), one of the oldest and most beautiful in a city renowned as a centre of Greek faith. There, he has devoted a life to studying music and writing books, applying Athonite monastic wisdom to contemporary concerns of alienation, depression, and isolation in his writings -  which also feed directly into his extraordinary music. 

On a dozen songs the Holy Father proves as fluidly adept at a range of traditional Byzantine instruments (qanun, oud, cümbüş, Politikon tanbur, yali tanbur, ney, zurna, clarinet, Politiki lyra, Pontic lyra, kabak kemane) as his signature fretless guitar, favoured for its ability to feel out microtones - semi or quarter-tone pitches - closest to the human voice. The result is a level of emotional expression and harmonic colour that often escapes western modes, transcending a range of Asia Minor and Mediterranean styles from maqam to Greek traditional and Byzantine music with a disciplined but rapturous sense of transcendence.

Suffice it to say it all adds up to one of the most singular recordings we’ve heard in recent memory, knocking our heads clean off with flashbacks to the likes of Sandy Bull’s modal psych-folk, or even Sunn O))) x Julian Cope and Sun City Girls/Sir Richard Bishop ritualism in the first half, and traversing in the 2nd to astonishing sorts of techno impressionism, as with the THX string shear and choral chant of ‘TECHNO σε ΜΟΝΑΣΤΗΡΙ’ and a whole new definition of trance-techno, thru to bits that sound like a Greek Enya. 

100% brilliant, out there music.

Classy haul of dancehall and street soul-adjacent Zouk from the Caribbean isles, cooked up by Disques Debs, Radio Nova, and Tropical Discoteq programer Émile Omar. Check for the orchestral dates and raggo Créole flow of ‘Mwen inmin’ by Metal Sound; the syrupy sway of Claudy Siar and O’Taïm gems; the low-slung rap of X’Taz.

“Back to the golden nights of zouk clubs, where hip-hop, kompa, zouk and Caribbean grooves ruled the dance-floor. This selection documents a pivotal moment : a time when zouk was still not a fixed genre, but more a place, an atmosphere, somewhere people went to dance. It captures the spirit of an era: its creative effervescence, musical freedom, and the diversity of artists who shaped it. The very concept of “Kaz A Zouk” perfectly encapsulates this idea: a space where all styles could meet.”

The crème de la crème of Gallic dubbers - Full Circle, Froid Dub, Krikor, and Shelter - tactfully diffuse the heady tekkerz of ‘80s French “ethno-industrial” legends Vox Populi!, whose catalogue of wonders continues to inspire wayward musicks...

Emotional Response task four of VP!’s roughly spiritual descendants to redress their music in a dubwise slipstream of style & pattern; stretching out from Alexis Le Tan & Joakim’s modal, early ‘90s-like Sannyacid Dub on the cusp of ‘Windowpane’-era Coil or The Orb, while Froid Dub bathe ‘Jube Man’ in a deep digidub recalling Sheriff Lindo oddities.

Pivotal Parisian producer Krikor follows in a vein of turbo-charged steppas from his Youth 7” to really send ‘Zen-Dub’ stratospheric, shades away from Element or TNT Roots, and Shelter reduces ‘Micro Climac’ to bubbling residue in step with his works for Séance centre and Emotional Response’s ‘’Checkmate in Dub’ session.

items.body:
Pushing back against "Acid Nostalgia", Lawrence English dreams of a moonlit future on 'The Rest is My Ghost', bringing in assistance from a heap of collaborators, including Mats Gustafsson, Tony Buck, Chris Abrahams, Rully Shabara, Norman Westberg and Lena Ito.

Having fully deconstructed his persona on 2022's 'Approach', looking back to his formative influences - William Gibson's 'Neuromancer' and Yoshihisa Tagami's sci-fi manga 'Grey' - English was left with a conundrum that he solved by taking a step back. Last year's 'Even the Horizon Knows its Bounds' was billed as a grand collaborative effort, performed by a litany of English's associates and imagined as an "atmospheric tint" for the Naala Badu building at the Art Gallery of New South Wales. 'The Rest is My Ghost' is very different; more radical and more overtly political than its predecessors, more in line with 2014's charged 'Wilderness of Mirrors' and its brilliant follow-up 'Cruel Optimism', the album takes aim at the contemporary obsession with nostalgia. Provoked by a conversation with Adam Curtis and driven by texts from Mark Fisher, JG Ballard, Katsuhiro Otomo, Franco Berardi, Kate Crawford and Alexie Yurchak and cultural architectural realities like the loss of Los Angeles' signature street lamps and Japan's Metabolists, English searches for a "political projection of nostalgia" that he can subsequently rupture. "Like acid poured onto a surface," he writes. "this use of nostalgia seeks to erode and smooth out the complexity and texture of lived connection and longing, which has until recently guided contemplations of nostalgia."

He's talking about the difference between dreaming of your own past and being sold a neatly packaged pseudo-reality, its highs and lows removed to ease the ingestion. Nobody would argue that 'Stranger Things', for example, wasn't nostalgic, but is its high concept fun comparable with any of its direct influences? Even its soundtrack pales alongside pretty standard straight-to-VHS fodder of the era, it's just cleaner, zippier and more shareable. And the more it dragged on, the less vital it became - a Gen X-core soap opera with eerily familiar visual cues. To represent this concept musically, English moves away from the dense distortions you might expect and instead collects up instrumental performances from a wide swathe of players. But perusing the personnel list and projecting your expectations on the material is part of the process. English obscures everything very purposefully, shrouding the instrumentation in reverb and midnight gusts. If seeing names like Swans' Thor Harris and pedal steel player Chuck Johnson gives you pause, that's the point. English engages in his own hauntological process, extracting the essence from the stems and imprinting it on his soundscapes. He's not eroding the material by any means, but searching out the triggers that play on the imagination, inspiring futures that have never been more difficult to grasp.

And if it sounds dark, it's really not supposed to. Listen through the nocturnal hums and gentle, thrumming ambiance and you'll discover more than you bargained for - even a glimmer of hope. The result is a record that lands somewhere between Les Disques du Crépuscule's post-classical gear, Eno's fourth world experiments with John Hassell and Alan Lamb's influential sound art.

items.body:
Remastered reissue of This Heat’s hugely innovative and pioneering anti-rock classic, 1979,  this time on their own, eponymous label. A true milestone in the mutation of pop, rock, avant-garde and electronic music, and arguably post-punk's ground-zero, This Heat consolidated a wealth of music before its arrival whilst casting irrevocable influence over a generation of musicians, producers and engineers in its wake.

Formed in mid ‘70s Brixton, South London, around the trio of Charles Hayward, Charles Bullen and Gareth Williams (later of Flaming Tunes fame), the group drew on and experimented within a flux of sonic disciplines - concrète, pop, dub, and krautrock - to align their mutual ligaments and oppositional structures in a complex, dissonant mass of finely edited improvisations.

Spooling tape noise Testcards jar abruptly with bursts of taut, buzzing drums and metallic guitar squall in Horizontal Hold, before Williams appears as a lamenting ghost, wallowing in the funereal folk drone of Not Waving, and like Damo Suzuki’s shy opposite against the motorik flight of Twilight Furniture.

The album’s definitive moment is still to come, however, with the 2-bar lick of Hayward’s propulsive drums spun thru devilish reverbs and delays in the legendary 24 Track Loop marking a pivotal moment in flux between dub, punk and electro-acoustic music, before the record closes out with Fall of Saigon’s melancholy dirge pop, which clearly set a template for everyone from Hot Chip to Animal Collective or Micachu and the Shapes.

Perhaps understandably, This Heat were never intended as a commercial proposition but, thru the support of John Peel they were able to reach and beguile a national radio audience who probably weren’t ready for them. Thus, their boundary-oblivious virus was planted in the fertile minds of ’79, when punk had already eaten itself and new ideas were definitely required.

By using a minimalist, rhythmically-focussed palette, rent by great minds using the studio-as-instrument, This Heat represents a crucial transition or phase-shift in music from stratified styles toward a union of what might have been formerly perceived as mutually exclusive sounds or styles; boldly following a path out of genre restriction and dilating the dimensions of sonic possibility in the process.

A stone cold classic.

items.body:
Compiling rare-as-hen's-teeth material from iconic Aotearoa/New Zealand label World Resources, 'Fully Nowhere' presents four sides of scuzzy lo-fi rock, drone, noise pop and improv from a tight cadre of the country's most prolific outsiders.

Established in the 1990s in Wellington, World Resources was a DIY label that specialised in tapes and micro-edition lathe-cut 7" singles and the home of Donald Smith, Paul Toohey and Tony McGurk's long-running free noise/drone band Surface of the Earth. It's an imprint that helped impact its region's knottiest outsider surges, so World of Echo does us a favor here by scraping together some of its rarest and most enduring sides, assembling a 25-track collection of some of the best basement drone and most surreal noise pop that's ever emerged from the Southern Hemisphere. The anthology begins in 1994 with two 7"s from Gorgecop, a short-lived solo project from Toohey. And already we're in impressive territory, with slashy grot-rock gear that wouldn't be out of place alongside The Shadow Ring and waved kosmische synth experiments that have more in common with the Dusseldorf wave. 

Donald Smith's Lucky Stars project yanks us back down to earth with the surprisingly bright and breezy 'Winter Call' a track that's so deliciously lo-fi that its drum machine beat barely cracks a faint pulse. Side B houses the grimy 'Hospital' and 'Smell of a Man's Room' from McGurk's Sewer solo project, tracks that originally appeared in 1995 on lathe cut of just 20 units that apparently never left his flat, and New Zealand Guitar Orchestra, a collaborative project between Surface of the Earth and Dress, have their two album releases condensed into a long stretch of submerged noise and interference that's worth the asking price alone. Of course, Surface of the Earth have to appear at some point and their track 'Shield' rounds up the side, with the brilliantly faded 'Commandcom' opening the next. Here, the trio's work is contextualized alongside their solo experiments, work as K-Group, Sewer and Destrifan that helps piece together a past, present and future of three DIY icons.

items.body:
Roy Montgomery and Martha Skye Murphy extend their thing on 'Nebular', penning a suite of widescreen dreampop epics that harness all their separate strengths into a fizzing artmelt -  tipped FFO Cocteau Twins & Harold Budd, Flying Saucer Attack, Jessamine and lovesliescrushing.

It didn't take much for Montgomery and Murphy to connect. All Murphy did was include one of Mongomery's songs on a mixtape and the conversations that followed led them to spot harmonies in their approaches to music: they both recorded to a Tascam multitrack recorder, for one. And if you've been following either artist, you'll have noticed their collaborations bubbling up through the cracks in the last few years. Murphy appeared on Montgomery's lush 'At Dawn' lathe cut 7" in 2023 and on his 2024 Roy Montgomery and Friends album 'Broken Heart Surgery (An Agony In Six Fits)', while Montgomery lent his distinct tone to Murphy's 2024 debut album 'Um', playing on the excellent 'Need'. It was all leading up to 'Nebular'; the two artists might be based on opposite sides of the globe, with Montgomery in New Zealand and Murphy in the UK, but they sound fully converged on this perfectly-pruned five tracker, developing a sound that's both related to their respective solo signatures and presents something new, too.

Montgomery's well-worn tone is present, forming a pillowy bed of post-Florian Fricke ambiance, yet it doesn't sound like any of his recent releases. And although Murphy's powerful, operatic tones were just as crucial to the success of 'Um', they're used differently here, reshaped into elongated, wordless traces and textures. Somehow, as weighty as it is, it works like a lengthy introduction before 'Nebular' asserts itself in earnest on 'Cloudburst'. Singing more confidently, Murphy augments her breathy vocals with stacked, dreamy textures that wisp and wind around Montgomery's strums. Maybe we can link it to Grouper or possibly even Julia Holter, but the way the duo treat the mixing and recording makes it sound older and grungier, like some lost 4AD release that never made it to the pressing plant.

The record hinges around the 17-minute 'The Play of Light and Dark', a side of rhythmic, chiming ambience from Montgomery that Murphy helps sculpt into a muggy mantra, vocalising unrestrainedly and shaping a sound that's refreshingly human. It doesn't shift so much as it melts, changing only slightly to draw you into its aura. When Mary Lattimore shows up on the finale 'At Dusk', it's a gorgeous, necessary palate cleanser.

In physical stature and imaginative scope, Luc Ferrari’s 10 x CD / 11 Hour selection for INA GRM’s series presents a poetic building block of C.20th electronic music from the founding director of the GRM in 1958, presenting a unique art history spanning six decades of ingenious, beguiling soundcraft.

Part of a legendary series including titles by concrète pioneers Pierre Schaefer & Pierre Henry, plus weighty surveys of Bernrad Parmegiani, Éliane Radigue and François Bayle, this lavish boxset of Luc Ferrari’s work is a masterclass exploration of avant garde form and function that charts experimental music’s research and development during a radical phase. While even the notion of such a large storage device for sound was unimaginable when Ferrari began making his cut-up musical collages and sound poetry in the ‘50s, his ‘L’Œuvre Électronique’ covers the progression of musical technology and thought from its most laboriously executed origins, working with tape and raw blocks of sound, to the grander digital staging of his ‘90s and early ‘00s radio plays, plotted for multiple voices and spatialised landscapes. 

Collected, this set forms an incredible deep dive into art-music history where the materiality of sound is questioned and reconsidered in relief of its musical connotations, creating in the process a peerless body of work that better approximates the texture of dreams or the audness of waking life than any song, and has long informed the approach to sound organisation by a host of progressive artists, effectively bridging the conceptual precedents of Varèse and Cage and the contemporary futures projected by Lee Gamble or Valerio Tricoli.

The 98 tracks from 31 releases, clocking up just over 10 hours of recordings, delineate across decades following Ferrari’s studies with Messaien and Honegger in the mid ‘50s, and a period of illness that made him better acquainted with the radio receiver, and pioneers such as Schöneberg and Webern, to his co-founding of the Groupe de Recherches Musicales with Schaeffer and François-Bernard Mâche in 1958, and thru his landmark transformation of field recordings made on a Yugoslavian beach, and the ravishing abstractions of later electronic works. 

Until his passing, aged 76 in Arezzo, Italy, Ferrari remained ceaselessly active both in his own practice and teaching, and was revered as the poet of musique concrète. He bought a particularly gallic purview to the paradigm, especially when considered against the more hard-nosed academic pursuits of his peers, making singular use of vocals as an elusive or sometimes literal presence in his works in a way that others didn’t, and as such his works all hare a certain liminal quality that appears richly seductive to fans of fantasy storytelling as much as psychedelic soundtracks and sound as dreamfood imagery.

items.body:
Greek harpist and composer Sissi Rada interprets the music of Richard Wagner and Johannes Brahms with unfathomable levels of detail and charm, resulting in one of the most gorgeously executed records of the year. Trust - it’s fully essential listening FFO Joanna Newsom, Svitlana Nianio, Kate Bush, Delphine Dora, Nikos Mamangakis…​

Sissi Makropoulou has been pinging our radar for a while now, but especially hard since 2024's Stroom-released 'Aporia' and that dazzling ‘Demeter In Aexone’ album that properly locked us in to her brand of uncanny avant dream-folk, a highly distinctive signature sound she developed even further on the fantastic 'Nana Butu' earlier this year. She’s a serial collaborator - with Lena Platonos, Brian Eno, Christina Vantzou, Jay Glass Dubs -  even Lee "Scratch" Perry -  all the while composing chamber music on the side. And It's that latter practice that comes to the fore on ‘Serious Songs’ singing in German while attacking Wagner's chilly 'Fünf Gedichte für eine Frauenstimme' (Five Poems for a Female Voice) on the A side, and Brahms' pious 'Vier ernste Gesänge' (Four Serious Songs) on the flip. As you'd expect, it isn't just a simple recital; with harp and voice the focal points, packed out with winding, nebulous arrangements and perspicacious references to avant-garde musical history, integrating dissonant orchestral elements, prepared piano, opera, classical guitar, environmental sounds and foreboding oscillations  - with an exquisite ear for detail.

Oddly for music this tranquil, it benefits from increased volume - at least a level where you can marvel at the array of tiny, unusual production flourishes. And it's a suite that grows and grows. On 'Wesendonck 1’, she opens with voice and harp recalling Joanna Newsom's folk-inspired song cycle 'Ys'. But as the piece develops, she begins to slowly show her hand, introducing harmonic, hypnotic effects to blur the edges. The result is discombobulating in the best way, sounding as dreamy as Julee Cruise's 'Floating into the Night' while somehow still remaining true to the source material. The drama continues to build on 'Wesendonck 2', her delivery of the words - written by poet Mathilde Wesendonck who Wagner was famously besotted with - fittingly dramatic, assisted by brass and grinding drums broken occasionally by moments of ineffable beauty. On 'Wesendonck 4', Makropoulou augments the production with metallophone chimes, fixing sequences with growling synths and heavily processed cries.

Sissi plays a remarkable sleight of hand on the flip. Beginning conservatively, she introduces Brahms' cycle of Lutheran biblical readings with a celestial harp and a gently experimental vocal, pitch shifted to a screwed conclusion. On 'Brahms 2', her performance is kinked by disorienting concrète-style operatic spools that pull us into another musical timeline entirely. She is so confident with her subject matter - whether it's the classical canon, folk, electronic or neue musik - that it all sounds like a natural extension of her practice, converging into something that fully defies categorisation.

Anyway, words don’t really do it for this one. Just give it a spin and you’ll soon melt into it, one of the most quietly startling albums released this year.

The classic 12 disc Parmegiani Box Set finally given a reissue by INA GRM, covering the majority of Parmegiani's musique concrète output recorded between 1964 and 2007. Is there a more important, influential, totemic single-artist collection in all of electronic music?

The Wire magazine described it as a "bargain price treasure chest....containing worlds of inexhaustible spaciousness and strangeness" and, indeed, listening through just some of the 12 cd's included you find yourself drawn into a multi-faceted world full of timeless treasure.

Parmegiani was mentored by the founding father of Musique Concrète, Pierre Schaeffer, who made use of technological advances that gave the world magnetic tape and microphones to pioneer a method taking everyday noise and transforming them into unrecognisable sounds, a style that became known as Acousmatic music. 

Parmegiani would go on to make use of these Acousmatic techniques in creating a body of work which is not only one of the most significant of the 20th century, but also hugely influential on a whole host of musical pioneers that would follow in his wake, with Christian Fennesz, Aphex Twin, Kode9 and Jim O'Rourke being notable disciples in the contemporary field. 

It’s hard to comprehend let alone articulate the immersive and often woozy effect of these recordings, ranging from eerie cut-out tape loops through to popular music plunderphonics and proto-distilled-dub that's impossible to absorb in one sitting. In short, L’Œuvre Musicale is one of the most impressive and important collections of electronic music you'll likely ever hear, but also one of the most rewarding.

The Necks regroup on a staggering first new LP in three years, switching between skittering jazz to widescreen rollers with a breathtaking momentum - somewhere between classic Verve label, MvO Trio, This Heat and Oren Ambarchi's ensemble jams.

The Necks’ Chris Abrahams (piano, Hammond organ), Tony Buck (drums, percussion, electric guitar) and Lloyd Swanton (bass guitar, double bass) re-ignite a mesmerising minimalism on ‘Travel’, taken from very lightly edited and overdubbed recordings of their daily 20 minute warm-up/improv practice sessions. Now in their 34th year playing together, the Aussie unit’s fine-honed intuitions are fully apparent across four durational parts totalling 77 minutes sprawling across seemingly endless soundscapes that collapse into myriad genres.

Perfectly framed and suspended with beautifully buoyant mixing and engineering by long time collaborator Tim Whitten, ‘Travel’ is a swaggering statement by the modern masters of long-form jams. The elements are knit with a particularly smoked-out verve and swingeing flex in each part, stretching from what sounds like MvO Trio haunted by Jackie Mittoo on the extraordinary ‘Signal’, to an uncanny, streamlined echo of Ndikho Xaba and the Natives’ South African free jazz on ‘Forming’, before resembling Can emulating Brazilian jazz on ‘Imprinting’, and arriving at the heart-in-mouth tempest of snare rolls, escalating organ vamps and roving low end that brings the LP to a thunderous climax like some extended Alice Coltrane breakdown that leaves u tossed in mid air.

Sounding as lean and potent as they did on 1989’s debut LP ‘Sex’, they’re frankly showing off here, with ‘Travel’ registering as good a place as any to kick off your infatuation with one of the world’s greatest experimental units.

items.body:
Enigmatic label/collective life is beautiful fully establishes its lore on a colossal 3LP sprawl: 39 tracks of whimsical outsider biz arcing from lo-fi strums to asymmetric pop, jazz improv, poetry, noise, abstract hip-hop, spoken word and whatever else captures the thing, from artists you'll know and a fair few you won’t, featuring Bianca Scout, aloisius, VOICE ACTOR, James Massiah, Kenichi Iwasa, THE NARRATOR, Isaiah Hull, Pretty V and many, many more.

A self-styled gesamtkunstwerk, life is beautiful was established by aloisius in 2022 as a radio show, before turning into a collective, a series of live performances, and then inevitably a record label a year later. Their first comp makes some attempt to pull all their various strands into something cohesive, but like many of the best collectives - Mica Levi’s Curl crew for example - so much of the beauty and joy comes from following the breadcrumb trail deep into wherever they take you. This is a label, after all, that dumped their demos and experiments ("resources and inspiration") on a file exchange portal on their own site, so you get the idea that nothing is quite fixed, and there are no easy answers - just the pleasure of tagging along for the ride.

The set opens with tracks from each of the founders, who establish the label's core sound. NWAKKE begins with 'i need you in a positive way', a cloudy hypnagogic R&B marvel that juxtaposes cool-headed vocal runs with tape-fucked field recordings and piano. Then, the mic's handed to Amber Joy, aka THE NARRATOR, who also serves as the label's artistic director; on 'SUDDENLY', she oozes a skittish post-everything collage that chops cheap synths and choral vocals into a dreamy modern hymn. aloisus' 'you are god' runs out of its stuck groove as if it emerges from the very same thought, blurring gospel moans across LinnDrum loops. Bianca Scout hands us a taster of her collaborative work with London's Cajm on the hypnotic 'Welcome to Hello', while poet Isaiah Hull teams up with y+Your for the wonked 'vampire money'.

Basically there's a whole record of music from the crew before 'veneration...' even begins in earnest, and it only gets better from here, running through aesthetic experiments from multi-instrumentalist Kenichi Iwasa, self-styled "beat wizard" psychedelic ensemble. (who's one half of Brum's Everything is Psychedelic with Tony Bontana) and Thom Dehli before we reach the compilation's crown jewel, a 21-minute live jam from okk70 ensemble. We can't tell you exactly who's playing, but it's worth the price of entry alone, a squirming slo-mo jazz side that gets to the roots of the life is beautiful sound - like some cross between ’87 era Prince and Oren Ambarchi’s Ghosted Trio, except deep in the basement. Elsewhere, there's a chewably eccentric solo moment from Bianca Scout ('superscribe 24'), a phenomenally moody collaboration between VOICE ACTOR and aloisius ('24'), a spirited, lo-fi transmission from London's josiane pozi and a deeper than deep jam from orchestra379, aloisius' "collective improvisation project" that's featured artists like Ben Vince, Kenichi Iwasa and abi asisa. 

Label comps are often a slog but this one's stuffed to the gills with genuinely creative experimentation from some of the scene's most interesting outsiders, the sprawl really does come close to harnessing the vibe.

Avon’s lesser-hailed, glam ‘80s synth-pop and new wave movement is spotlighted in-depth via 20 songs compiled by studio engineer Dave Massey, who smartly portrays the breadth and quality of an ‘80s blindspot.

‘The Bristol & Bath Blitz Club Meets Art School Sound - 80's Explosion’ traces the reverberating influence of Rusty Egan and co.’s new wave crucible, The Blitz Club, along the M4 leyline, where it met Avon art school kids advancing from punk and funk into a new decade. Egan’s signature DJ brew - e.g. Kraftwerk to Visage, Burundi Black to Bowie, Japan and Grace Jones - would spark myriad emulators who were also mirroring the chops of Duran Duran (sons of the Brum club scene an hour north) and the likes of Martyn Ware et al in Sheffield, in their blends of US funk, European machine music, and a punky license to follow their nose. 

Fair to say it’s not the usual tale of Bristol’s dub-rooted and punk heritage. Between Distant Cousins’ Arabic-inflected new wave ace ‘Red Oasis’, and the angular chops of ‘Your Heart My Ambition’ from Frame By Frame, it checks for a spectrum of pop moxie taking in the swooning goth pop of Great Naked; BEF-meets-Bowie pomp of Wadi Vision; Nite Watch and glaxobabies’ disco-boogie; a stranger standout of synth sleaze by Startled Insects; Duran Duran-esque new wave funk by Creature Beat; and a ballad pearl by The Escape - all sure to mess with preconceptions of Bristol history.

Key Chicago house architect Ron Trent departs the club for the bedroom under new alias La Marr, a new vent for his most romantic, sublime soundscapes, warmly advised FFO Detroit Escalator Company, Terre Thaemlitz, Wally Badarou, Klaus Schulze, MvO Trio

Light candles/incense and scatter petals for optimal effect when immersing in La Marr’s debut ‘Mood Programs’ EP, which finds a perfect home nestled amid Music From Memory’s precious, timeline-twining cuts of new age ambient, kosmiche, and Balearic wist. It’s also a natural, logical progression from the sort of depths usually secreted in Trent’s albums, but here given full sides to unfurl their functions, which we’re sure will also sound dead tasty, syrupy slow, on 33-not-45. 

He paints the lushest 12 min panorama of elliptical stereo pads, floating organ cloud structures and skin-stroke arps in ‘Good Magic’, edging on similar terrain to Terre Thaemlitz’s golden revision of Tangerine Dream’s ‘Love on a Real Train’, where a fine line of hand played drums emphasises the swaying groove - swooning either bed-ways or a little rug-cut, depending on your disposition - before ‘Clear’ hustles a palette of the slinkiest Afro-Latinate, Brazilian rhythms under big, dusky skies, hinting at Manuel Göttsching via MvO Trio. 

Your ears do not deceive you: this one is proper lush.

items.body:
jason calhoun’s fifth release for Dear Life Records,

"On revelations of divine love Calhoun has assembled an especially potent album of work that whirrs, hums, and glows. Unlike his recent output centered around extended, hypnotic compositions, the fourteen tracks here immediately request your attention and curiosity. Their concision only underscores one of his greatest strengths: the ability to capture an evaporating, fleeting moment, and hold it close.

The title is a nod to British Anchoress Julian of Norwich, whose collected writing of the same title is the earliest of any woman written in English. Here it serves as a unifying theme for Calhoun's particular palette of restless textures and tentative melodies. This is personal music, to be sure, but it also feels tactile, almost taffy-like in its presentation—and with such a potent combination, it is hard to resist a smile while listening. Like when the insistent pulse grounding 'last one' suddenly changes color as yawning tones reveal themselves, or how 'eye dilation' tiptoes into the room with each note sounding like a carefully chosen step. Though never precious or fussy, the album remains resolutely intimate.

Calhoun puts it plainly: “Julian of Norwich says “‘All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well’. These days, I’ve been having my doubts that this is true. As no solution to the issue at hand, I look for the revelations of divine love in my life, and I find them--in my partner asleep on the floor in our studio, my survival of a social interaction with a stranger, being bad at chess. Don't ask me what they mean-I'm still figuring that out myself. Maybe we can figure it out together.” It is from this place of doubt, searching, and openness that the album finds its footing."

TTT tack to classical chamber music with the intimately fuzzy recital of richly melodic works written between mid-14th and 21st centuries and performed by NYC’s Cop Tears, a trio of early and avant garde music specialists; Derek Baron, Cameron kapoor, and John Andrew Wilhite.

Attending to an emergent TTT touchstone of recent times - as in Jack Sheen’s works, thru aspects of Will Bankhead’s What We and Guild mixes - Cop Tears lean into interests in quieter chamber music laced with threads of lo-fi, folk and jazz that tie ‘The Rules of the Game’ to the label’s key corpus. The 13 pieces follow five years from the trio’s ‘Theodor Adorno: Piano Works’, and five again from their debut ‘Thirteen Harmonies (1986) Selections From John Cage’s ‘Apartment House 1776’’, with enchanting slants on cherry picked pieces that endure, some over 600 years later, on the strength of their timeless arrangements.

In key with the label's thing, everything is swaddled in ferric gauze - possibly posited on auld tape recorders - and holds a peculiar, homely, discordant charm (including fits of giggles and room noise) for the duration, which never tests the patience. The C.14th, polyphonic chanson Ars Nova masterpiece of Guillaume de Machaut ‘Puis qu’en oubli’ is the set’s oldest, along with ‘Quam pulchra est’, a mid-C.15th work for recorder trio by John Dunstable, placed on the same page with the more angular chamber jazz modernism of ‘Selections from Piano Sonata after a Conversation with Jonathan Gean (2016)’ and their take on the naïf wooze of ‘Children's Music, No. 1, II: Modern Dance (1973)’ by Valentin Silvestrov. Our percy is the dreamy, creaking baroque elegance of ’S’io men vo (1618)’, but it’s best advised to take it all in one at your leisure...

items.body:
First re-pressing in years of Mark Ernestus & Moritz Von Oswald’s divine, final Rhythm & Sound release, heeling to tradition with a one-riddim album focussed on its carousel of roots reggae legends; Sugar Minott, Paul St. Hilaire, Willi Williams, Jah Cotton, Bobbo Shanti, and more

In 2005 Rhythm & Sound capped their holy mountain catalogue with ‘See Mi Yah’, a 7 x 7” set and LP which completed a 10 year run of inspired dub productions with their purest offering to the form. At the time, younger ears to their music would be left perplexed by the lack of instrumental variation - but any others with a little knowledge of one-riddim set traditions knew it was their ultimate ode to roots reggae fundamentals, after respectfully messing with the style & pattern across the Burial Mix 10”s (as collected in ‘w/ The Artists’), and the more radical 12” mutations of the Rhythm & Sound series, proper, since 1996 (not to mention birthing dub house-techno before that).     

Seeing off the project in fine style, Ernestus & Von Oswald gave studio time to their favourite vocalists, generating a slew of original performances displaying the range and depth of roots reggae’s elders and contemporary torch carriers on their signature backdrop of air-trodding bass and powdered dub chords. We were blessed to distribute it in the UK at the time, so many of these cuts are hard etched to the memory, from the ghostly croon of Willi Williams’ title piece thru the gruff gravitas of Bobbo Shanti, the duet between Ras Donovan & Ras Perez, and of course Sugar Minott’s mellifluous reggae soul.

In the year following ‘See Mi Yah’, Rhythm & Sound were naturally elected to edit and master a re-up of The Congos & Friends’ one-riddim album ’Fisherman Style’ for our then warehouse neighbours Blood & Fire Records, sealing their era of roots reflection by appropriately saluting the originators, in parallel to their Wackies reissue scheme, and before Ernestus (and Mark Ainley) would go on to found the more digi-devoted reissue label, Dug Out. Some 20 years of satisfaction later, time has proven this album holds its meditative weight.

items.body:
Effortlessly easy on the ear and yet still somehow fathoms-deep, Tara Clerkin Trio’s latest is their most refined and fully-formed transmission yet, mining a precious sweetspot between chamber-jazz, Plone-style bric-a-brac electronics, Crescent’s lo-fi reveries and the urban pressure of the Young Echo collective, unpicking decades of British musical history in the process. Trust, it’s a special one.

Like every great band, TCT know their history. They've grown up with and formed their identity in the shadow of Bristol's musical lore, whether it's The Pop Group, Massive Attack or Flying Saucer Attack, and when they use traceable elements, it feels like a believable part of their DNA. Thankfully, they meaningfully add to that narrative too, not adapting an aesthetic for easy consumption. Part of this might be down to their makeup; they formed in the late 20-teens from the ashes of the Tara Clerkin Band, a larger ensemble that Clerkin had put together to expand the scope of her folk-y pop compositions. And when most of the members moved on, stepbrothers Sunny-Joe Paradiso and Patrick Benjamin stuck around to see where the road might lead. All "proper" players, they've traditionally let their songs appear from what sounds like loose, casual improvisations, like you're tuned into Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society' band running through Laika's 'Silver Apples of the Moon'.

So you get a song like the brilliant 'Ups & Downs', that simmers for a good four minutes with wheezing harmonium, double bass and clarinet, percussion just rumbling in the background somewhere, before a jerky sampled beat, Mellotron strings and Clerkin's voice would have you thinking Matt Elliott's behind the boards. But 'Somewhere Good' is also remarkably tight when it needs to be, walking a tightrope between easy breezy and meticulous with acrobatic skill. Opener 'Lake Walk', for example, sounds intentionally naive, jammed out loosely on synthesised and real woodwind that's caught in a vortex of Space Echo, before 'Lazy Daisy' cuts it short with its more ordered (but still kinda slouchy) beat-heavy dreampop atmosphere. It's where the album's shape really coagulates, between Broadcast's dramatic early EPs (back when they were touring with Plone) and Pram's best shit, just lightly tweezed at the edges, its creases relaxed to fit in with Laila Sakini's quietly genius 'Paloma'. And that mood carries the record even when Clerkin's voice - pursed into a soulful croon or a lackadaisical murmur - vanishes completely. One of the most gripping moments arrives with 'There Was a Nice Sunset', effortlessly matching slowcore drums with piano flourishes and synths, locking into the same general feeling but widening the boundaries, nodding to Adrian Sherwood's lysergic work on Creation Rebel's 'Starship Africa'. 

There's years of British musical history baked into this stuff, and yet it feels wholly new.

items.body:
Produced by Neek and Jabu's Amos Childs (aka O$VMV$M), Manonmars' third album is syrupy suite of smoke-hazed recollections and free associated reflections set to decelerated bumps, sluggish samples and cloudy drones = sturdy biz FFO Young Echo, Massive Attack, Cold Light, Ka, MIKE, King Vision Ultra, Coby Sey.

Manonmars' 2018 debut is one of those albums we still go back to periodically. It's that rare meeting of minds: a space for O$VMV$M to flex their production muscle and a scratchpad for London-based MC, painter and photographer Jack Martyn Richardson to sketch out a distinct vision of England. And His experiences and impressions on 'Entertainment System' still feel chewable. "Goddess on my arm and both our phones got no service," he quips on 'Goddess'. "Acid is lysergic, psychedelic rock is Turkish." His rhymes aren't throwaway, they map out an underground that's very recognisable, shadowed by O$VMV$M's tuff, effective soundscapes - beats that reference trip-hop, ambient music, exotica and '70s movie soundtracks as much as they do US rap. 

On opener 'Flam3throw3r', Mars raps in double-time over shrill horns that blot out any trace of a beat; Neek and Childs sound as if they relish the negative space, adding chic sword swipes to a track that's got little else to do with the Wu Tang Clan. When a lumbering beat kicks in on 'Decathlon', flipping from downtempo to no-tempo in the final act, it sounds as if it's just there to assert O$VMV$M's commitment to slowness - Mars doesn't even seem to notice, rhyming casually but never losing his flow.

Bristol mainstays Franco Franco and Dali de Saint Paul turn up to assist on 'Volcanic Shield', one of the album's most conventional bangers, led by O$VMV$M's skittering Surf Gang-like beats and morse code blips, and cold light's Birthmark lends his voice to 'Infinite', going bar for bar with Mars over Neek and Childs' slackened funk, blaring out like an old tape on a busted in-car audio system. 'Firewater' takes the same approach, leaving Mars to do his best as snares splash across the spectrum with added sax from Brum-based sound artist Lorenzo Prati. "My bitch white, she can scuba dive and ice climb," he spits. "Put the drink down, I wasn't in my right mind." 

It's music that laughs through the tears - what could be more British than that?

One of the most influential, insular and multi-layered albums of the last five decades, created through endless hours of improvisation - involving almost fifty musicians and recorded in complete darkness, 'Spirit Of Eden' was a radical departure for Talk Talk, ' an album that has attained almost mythical status since its release in 1988.

Following the commercial success of their singles "It's My Life", "Life's What You Make It” and album "The Colour of Spring”, Talk Talk retreated into the shadows and produced an album that still defies categorisation. Mark Hollis is said to have demanded the players record in almost complete darkness, improvising for hours to produce individual parts without hearing any backing tracks or surrounding material.

"Spirit Of Eden" is one of the most fearless and rewarding leaps a commercially successful band has ever taken, and continues to cast its influence almost 40 years later.

On 'gg', Lolina reminisces about broken dreams and heartbreak. "That's one secret I will never tell," she promises, over smudgy, time-stretched drums and muggy organs. "Let's get another drink, or do you think I should be sober for what I am about to say?" It's a sonic side-eye that may or may not be historical and the lore's only extended by the cryptic press release (provided by Kaitlin Simotics) and the two reworks of Lolina's original.

London duo NEW YORK channel Lolina's energy into pop, singing the refrain and beefing the casual charm up with an electroid bassline, while Arca heads off-world, using Lolina's puzzling narrative to inspire her most gaseous track since her run with Björk. Digital harps are interrupted with glitches, and Lolina's words are slowed against syrupy OPN-like chipmunked chorals that coalesce into a symphonic crescendo...

items.body:
New LP from Californian singer/songwriter Luke Temple aka Art Feynman.

"Slow, unfussy, and largely instrumental, Orphans finds Art Feynman turning inward. Conceived as “music to do other things by,” the album is designed to live alongside daily activity, coloring the atmosphere without demanding focused attention. It moves through a space like wind chimes, less something to follow than something to feel. These are intimate, solitary explora- tions, sketches that feel less composed than discovered, yet they carry a quiet emotional clarity. Where Feynman’s past work often leaned on intricate grooves and dense interplay, Orphans is disarmingly still, patient, and comforting.

As the album begins, you can almost picture Feynman hunched over a 4-track, tracing melodies on a small Casio, following instinct wherever it leads. Opening track “Soft Reminder,” unfolds with a gentle organ line that's equal parts melancholy and curiosity, its tones lingering in the air rather than pushing forward, settling into the room as easily as it invites quiet reflection.

Elsewhere, “Soup Song” channels a kind of homespun minimalism, its insistent organ pattern recalling the early, exploratory spirit of Terry Riley’s A Rainbow in Curved Air. “Always In Need of Something” nods toward the playful, searching qualities of Francis Bebey, its cyclical phrasing suggesting a quiet, human restlessness beneath the surface. Throughout, tones and textures gently accumulate, shaping an atmosphere as much as a set of discrete compositions, subtly shifting the emotional temperature of whatever space they inhabit.

Late-album centerpiece “Ice Bath,” one of the few vocal moments, offers a subtle thesis: “It slowed me down / That’s what I needed / For a new beginning.” The song feels like a turning point, an acceptance of stillness as a necessary condition for change. It dissolves seamlessly into “The Condition of New Things,” a gorgeously skeletal electric guitar piece that lingers in open space, each note placed with careful intention, recalling some of Jeff Parker’s solo work.

Closing track, “Plastic Flowers,” drifts in on vocoder-softened vocals and a fragile bed of guitar and synth. “To trick the eye but still touch the heart,” Feynman sings, a line that quietly frames the album’s ethos. Like light shifting across a wall over the course of a day, these recordings may be modest, even illusion-like in their simplicity, but their emotional resonance is undeniable."

items.body:
Cathedral is a thrilling album and terrifying graphic novel from director and musician John Carpenter, based on a dream Carpenter had in 2024.

"An abandoned cathedral. A gruesome murder. A powerful supernatural entity living in the catacombs. It all comes to a head in downtown Los Angeles. What will happen and who will live to tell the tale? Such is the storyline of Cathedral, it has all the drama, dark atmosphere, and frenetic pacing of a classic heavy metal record. Especially designed as the soundtrack to the graphic novel, each track corresponds to a specific section of the book. The liner notes included with the album packaging feature prompts for each track, creating a fully interactive experience. Combined with the graphic novel, it’s the closest thing to a new John Carpenter film in years.

The music on Cathedral retains all the eerie atmosphere and sinister propulsion of the epochal scores Carpenter created for his films Halloween, The Fog, and Assault on Precinct 13, but this is a much heavier, riff-driven enterprise. Carpenter is a firm believer that music plays a major role in what really makes something scary. That’s first and foremost,” the director says. “It’s all about making the music work.” “This is somewhat different sounding stuff that we’ve done, but it’s done with the same desire in mind,” he adds. “In other words, put this thing on and imagine you’re watching a movie. That’s what we want you to do.”

Daniel Davies’ soaring, snaky guitars take center stage on opener “Primeval,” “Elevator,” and the metal masterpiece “Lord of the Underground” while John Carpenter and Cody Carpenter’s synths take the lead on the ominous “Desolation in the Underworld,” the plaintive “Death of the Mapmaker,” and even converge with strings on “Abandoned Cathedral.”

Whereas the Lost Themes albums were written as scores to movies of the mind, Cathedral scores the first original graphic novel written by Carpenter, his wife and long-time creative partner, producer and editor Sandy King, and writer Sean Sobczak, published by Storm King Comics."

items.body:
Pulling away from the taut beat science of 'Rhythm Archives' and his Sähkö stonker 'CRUX', Al Wootton sails confidently into hazed psychedelia on 'Rope', playing guitar, bass and clarinet alongside Italian free improv vet Irene Bianco's spirited freeform percussion.

Wooton's tenure in Holy Tongue, working alongside Valentina Magaletti and Susumu Mukai, has fully established him as a force to be reckoned with in the dub-void-fusion realm, but this one's way further out. We can only guess that he connected with Bianco, whose last solo jaunt was handled by Mageletti and Fanny Chiarello's Permanent Draft imprint, via Mageletti - but the result of this collaboration is very different from anything you'd expect from Holy Tongue. There are no guiding rhythms or identifiable grooves, instead both artists sound as if they're stroking the mood instead, figuring out what sounds they can overlay to conjure swirling spells of tone and texture. On opening track 'A/B', they come off like Joe McPhee and Milford Graves covering 'Laughing Stock', forming spirals of woodwind and percussion that Wootton nattily diverts with his arsenal of tape effects.

Bianco finds remarkably unexpected sounds from her modified drum kit, vibraphone and "other percussion instruments". But it's the relationship that the two artists manage to strike up that makes this much more then the sum of its parts. There's almost no beginning and no end - it's less about what each artist is doing exactly, more about the fully gelled sound that they're able to make. Listening to the title track, it's hard to believe it's improvised at all, sounding like it's been generated in some remote Italian studio for a dusty library LP that was discovered at the back of a damp Neapolitan basement.

String plucks nip between metallic resonances and croaks and voices chatter between breathy woodwind curlicues. Mid-way through, the volcano almost erupts when thudding rhythms rattle against distorted dissonances and a rumbling low end. The pair keep it reined in, never taking the obvious route and keeping us gripped throughout. Just peep the gong-led headmelt 'Spring', all eerie reverberations and off-world tape saturations, or 'Hara', a psychedelic dub-drone experiment that loses its all-important stabs in grubby vortexes of feedback. Recommended listening, no doubt.

His personal musical passion always was jazz, reflected in this deep selection of jazz works that were previously unavailable unless you had one of the few dozen copies pressed locally in the 1970s. The album doesn’t only highlight his musical statue as a composer but also as a outstanding trumpet soloists bringing together jazz, spiritual undertones and Malaysian folkloric themes balancing slower pacing deep, modal grooves with more upbeat jazz funk leanings.

Originally released on Sweat Lodge Guru back in 2011 before being reissued on vinyl two years later, Lee Noble's cult ambient-folk-synth milestone 'No Becoming' has finally been spruced up and remastered.

Nashville-born Noble had been parading around the US basement scene for a minute when he issued 'No Becoming', and the album stuck out like a sore thumb at the time. Packed out with VHS B-movie synth gear, freak'd-out psych jams, wyrd folk and groggy ambient moments, it wasn't really noise and didn't quite harmonize with the wave of Emeralds-adjacent kosmische revivalists, either. Now, it makes far more sense - so this reissue, that celebrates the Primordial Void label's eight year anniversary, feels perfectly timed.

Tune into the dirg-y opener 'Cop Show' and you might think you've stumbled over a lost '70s synth side - something in the vein of notorious "mail order mystic" Master Wilburn Burchette, dubbed to grubby cassette for ultimate fadedness. Then 'Paradise Life' takes a sharp left turn, stacking guitar drones into a euphoric mass and lavishing them with feedback and distortion. It's ambient, sorta, but not the kind that's capsized by its tendency to piss the sheets.

'Fantasy Hair', meanwhile, adds freeform drums and Wurlitzer vamps to accurately sketch out a locked Midwestern garage project and then 'Doesn't Matter What's Right' sounds like a humming folk revival project. It's all over the place, but it undoubtedly works.

Recorded live in Brooklyn, 'Somewhere in the Wind' is Loren Connors & David Grubbs’ third album and their first as a guitar duo, showcasing their free-er, noiser side with two extended, ecstatic jams. 

Thankfully, we didn't have to wait another two decades to hear Grubbs and Connors collide again. Their first album, 'Arborvitae', appeared way back in 2003, not long after the duo had first met when Connors shared a bill with Gastr del Sol. But it wasn't until 2024 that they rekindled that magic, shaking things up a little and swapping roles on keys and guitar, with Connors even moonlighting on drums. 'Somewhere in the Wind' might be the perfect companion to that record, recorded last year at Blank Forms, it's their first session featuring both players on electric guitar and it's a joy to engage with on every level. Both distinctive players carry an unmistakable signature style, complementing each other by leaning into the noise and freedom of their collaboration in a way we hadn't witnessed until now. 

If their first two records dug into crepuscular space, the domain of Roy Montgomery and Harold Budd, this one takes its cues from the physicality of their instruments and the knowledge they've acquired along the way. You feel as if you're practically in the room with them as Connors's blurry post-blues recitals casually interact with Grubbs' obsessively tuned intonations. On the first side, we walk into what might as well be a prayer, each note played in reverence to something or someone. But as the piece accumulates weight, so too do the notes, lovingly distorted and pushed off track until all that's left is raw emotion. On the flip, the duo sound even more possessed, kicking up the energy so the notes bounce around the very edges of the recording space. It's a document of two players who don't have anything left to prove.

items.body:
16 hours of peerless, important works by Eliane Radigue relating to her work with the ARP 2500 synthesiser between 1971-2000. Prior to this period, Eliane worked exclusively with feedback on tape and oscillators, but her work from the ‘70s onward is defined by an uniquely meditative and transcendent grasp of microtonal minimalism which has latterly come to place her among the 20th century’s most esteemed and truly inimitable composers. Bearing in mind that Eliane realised this fathomless body of work in her Paris apartment away from professional recording studios, only makes it resonate more strongly with the idea that Eliane was a genuine outlier whose uniquely sober work divined an unquantifiable yet ultimately human nature in electronic music. RIP legend.

"Eliane Radigue was born in Paris. She studied “musique concrète” techniques at the “Studio d’Essai” of the RTF under the direction of Pierre Schaeffer and Pierre Henry (1956-57). She was married to the painter and sculptor Arman and devoted ten years to their three children. She then worked with Pierre Henry, as his assistant at the Studio APSOME (1967-68). She was in residence at the New York University School of Arts (1970-71), the University of Iowa and the California Institute of the Arts (1973) and Mills College (1998). She has created sound environments using looped tapes of various durations, gradually desynchronising.

Her works have been featured in numerous galleries and museums since the late 60s and from 1970, she has been associated to the ARP 2500 Synthesizer and tape through many compositions from Chry-ptus (1970) up to L’Île resonante (2000). These include: Biogenesis, Arthesis, Ψ 847, Adnos I, II and III (70s), Les Chants de Milarepa and Jetsun Mila (80s) and the three pieces constituting the Trilogie de la Mort (1988-91-93). Since 2002, she has been composing mostly acoustic works for performers and instruments. Her music has been featured in major international festivals. Her extremely sober, almost ascetic concerts, are made of a continuous, ever-changing yet extremely slow stream of sound, whose transformation occurs within the sonic material itself.

Radigue found her musical voice through the decisive encounter with “musique concrète” and its founding fathers. With Pierre Schaeffer, first, and then Pierre Henry, with whom she learned and perfected the art of tape recorders. She then developed a unique style by herself, freely continuing the exploration of electronic sounds, progressing with tenacity through her musical quest, without worrying about current trends or fashions, paying no attention to creeds or dogmas. An isolated course, out with fashions and institutions, such a singular and intense music, so remote from everything..."

Collagist producer-DJ and Modern Love & PAN alum, Flora Yin-Wong maps rugged terrain between one-take drone noise, drill, R&G, and Thai TikTok tunes, for Liverpool’s roving, expansive label, SINK.

An hour-long mix melding original material with cuts that traverse the timeline from early R&G (the R&B-inspired grime style) to drill crud with a signature, dare-to-differ steez. The results feel like an impressionistic joyride across the contemporary soundscape, variously baring nastier fangs in its blast of thorny digital noise, and icy picks of drill, but always sure to resolve in more bittersweet sorts of ambient drone-pop with a mix-taper/collagist license.

To our lugs it conjures a night drive cruising past post-industrial wastelands to glittering new docksides, intercepting stray waves of the hard rap that’s lit a real fire in the Scouse belly of recent times, and backseat aux-cord/bluetoothing sounds from her social feeds. The addition of her own blasts of drone noise ideally punctuate and decouple the sequence from the prosaic to the poetic in hypnotic style.

Seoul’s Uman Thurman & Yetsuby, aka Salamanda, meditate on the inner life of a basil plant with a delicately flavoured suite of pottering pulses and harmonised warmth in a fine tradition of Far Eastern ambient electronica that chimes with label mates at GMT and the likes of E Ruscha V or Woo.

“The album moves through a full day in the plant's life opening with ‘introduce my atom which is my favorite one’, an act of quiet self-declaration in morning light, before settling into the unhurried rhythmic pulse of ‘to to ki toki tok’- the drip of water, the tick of a clock, the slow beat of photosynthesis. ‘allez, pousse!’ - one of the standouts in this journey - carries the basil's gentle will to grow, to push, to tilt toward the sun, while ‘hungry snail’ captures a moment of creaturely encounter on the glass: an uninvited visitor, moving slowly, wanting. As the afternoon deepens, 'Basil's Ritual' traces the daily ceremony of light and warmth, repeated with calm devotion from root to leaf. Night falls across 'Basil's Dream', and in the stillness something like sleep arrives - the plant resting, imagining tomorrow's sun. The album closes with ‘the blue wine’, a final mysterious reverie in which the basil seems to contemplate its own fate, somewhere between acceptance and wonder.”

items.body:
The Necks 18th album Vertigo is an eventful, kaleidoscopic tone poem set against a darkly shimmering background. Slowly but inexorably moving forward, it crosses many frontiers yet remains true to the mission and mood established in the opening stanzas of this cinematic 44 minute journey. A work able to be viewed either as a whole, or two symmetrical halves, Vertigo sees The Necks once again offer an excursion in sound that reflects both the light and darkness of some preternatural world. 

In contrast to the sustained improvisations that are their live performances, The Necks’ studio albums take shape by way of intricate crafting brought to bear throughout the entire recording and mixing process. “The discussion this time really began in earnest in the session itself, where we started to pursue the idea of having a drone running from start to finish, off which we could hang ideas,” said bassist Lloyd Swanton “But like all Necks albums we ended up in a very different place from whatever our initial notion of it had been.” 

Maintaining a teetering tension between suspension and collapse, Vertigo draws on a diverse palette of sounds created in the studio by Tony Buck (drums/percussion/guitar), Lloyd Swanton (bass) and Chris Abrahams (piano/keyboards), featuring everything from homemade instruments, extended instrumental techniques and marathon explorations of sonic textures. 

One piece, at the same time two. Monochrome, yet multicoloured. Dark, yet incandescent. Expansive and still. Melancholic and exhilarating. The Necks. Vertigo."

Selected and arranged by Jack Rollo and Elaine Tierney, Ballads’ is a waking-dream meander through beautiful, romantic, weird, exotic, intimate, un-categorisable music that shouldn't go together but yet somehow makes complete sense, offering a sort of spiritual life-enhancement in the process. 

A Colourful Storm’s Fleetway Tapes seems to has become the ideal place for skilled musical storytellers to flex their muscle, and on ‘Ballads’ the London-based duo turn their attention to the classic storytelling category of songcraft with the mix of forensic digging and poetic arrangement that has made their long-running NTS show a cult hit for many. Spanning a literate and cinematic world of sound with signature delicacy, they conjure a far flung and totally absorbing set whose track-listing remains impenetrable, and may well drive diggers to a tizzy. Suffice to say; numerous pearls lie within.

Sung in myriad tongues, the ballads range from the romantic and sentimental to the abstract and instrumental, spieling yarns that may not be fully understood, but with an atmosphere, pacing, and seductive vibe that's unmistakable.

For us, and so many, the mixtape of the decade.

items.body:
The Necks tantalisingly ruminate on stillness, decay and space in an absorbing, opiated follow-up to the windswept momentum of ’Travel’, chasing a quieter dragon into midnight airs shared by Loren Connors, Morton Feldman, that 'Autechre remix of Tortoise's 'To Day Retrieval', Talk Talk, Alice Coltrane.

Australia’s widely revered minimalist jazz / avant garde / electro-acoustic ambient (delete as applicable) troupe lure us right into the depths of their shared psyche with an unmissable invitation to swan the vast inner landscapes of ‘Bleed’. For an unbroken 42 minutes Chris Abrahams’ soft keys elide the shimmering plangency and distant, dreamlike drum rolls of Tony Buck and Lloyd Swanton’s painterly strokes of guitar at a seductive resting heart pace. Gently exploring notions of stasis, entropy, and space, and guided by an incandescent spirit that flickers between melancholy and the sublime, they trustingly navigate that schism with a subtlety that has propelled them since 1989’s classic ‘Sex’, and has left the template wide open for practically all Aussie experimental artists in their lustrous wake. 

Intimate yet expansive, ‘Bleed’ operates on a tongue tip of feeling in an almost palindromic arrangement that rewards repeat plays to supine minds. Chris Abrahams' grasp of extended melodic thought unfolds across the keyboard from right hand starlight to exquisitely sparing notes left to ring out on air like a syrupped Morton Feldman, gradually accreting the cross-hatching of Lloyd Swanton’s post-rock guitar hazes and bells carried on the warm air from Tony Buck, a usually ceentral figure who judiciously takes the back seat here.

Prone to leave languorous lacunæ for the imagination fills in the gaps, the piece proceeds into the most hauntingly sonorous mid section of layered, lingering overtones that hang over the atmosphere like noctilucent clouds, even precipitating a passage of atonal doom. However, they resolve via the padded palpitation of percussion at curiously bittersweet junctures in a coda that effectively leaves the keys to breeze and loop back to the start for anyone ready to go at it again. It’s typically gorgeous stuff, framing the trio at their lower case best.

On a ravishing first LP in five years, Arca continues to assume her ultimate form - an HR Giger-esque biomechanical entity; a psychopomp between virtual, physical, and mythological worlds - hallucinating a posthuman club music that feels like the future manifest in her mastery of queer-coded Latin dance and electronic music vernacular.

Leading on from the sprawling ‘Kick’ (2020-21) pentalogy, ‘XXXXX’ consolidates past and present Arca in a sheer vision of club possibilities. Within her 15 year catalogue, the 16-part album appears to balance the ruggedly bittersweet, exploratory spirit of 2013’s ‘&&&&&’ mixtape - a key touchstone of deconstructed dance music - with a more aggressive, yet romantic, thrust that’s emerged thru the ‘Kick’ volumes. Coupled with an ever-finer grasp of the advanced electronica practised by Æ or AFX (or E+E & T C F) which has long underlined her work, and the experience of sharpening her pop talons on Madonna, Rosalía and Kelela records, the results come to light as self-contained album of multitudes, bursting at the seams with fresh yet timeless ideas. 

With the benefit of hindsight it’s not hard to cite Arca as a pied piper of hyper-contemporary electronic music, one instrumental in altering its prevailing rhythmic currency to sexier tresillo permutations, whilst bringing back notions of alien pop in a lineage harking to Bowie via SOPHIE - metaphorically disrupting the status quo and physically changing the way people dance, and both on a really significant scale. ‘XXXXX’ now binds and frays all those strands in her most sharply defined and digestible album statement, eliciting a spectra of emotional responses and proprioceptive sensation with visionary tact and immersive sound design tekkerz.

Geared with a metric, melodic, and spatial freedom that owes to classical music as much as ‘90s electronica and 2010s DAW hyperprisms, the 16 parts unfold from theatric spectralism of ‘No End’, thru the gothic dembow deathknells of ‘Willow’ and fleet hoofed hyperpop of ‘Eidolon’ into singular takes on depth-charged doble paso reggaeton in ’Syncope’, and shearing Ae lines of extended melodic thought on ‘Raver’. A brisk centrepiece ‘Fxck’ is the LP’s horny club anthem in waiting, whilst ‘Finisher’ is maybe the freakier raver’s fave, for its tumultuous dramaturgy of tense strings and displaced braindance-drill trepanation, sharing a deadly torque with the scythe of ‘Grip’ and intense frisson delivered by the saccades of ‘Everything’. Knit with hyperpop prayer ‘Enraptured’, and symphony of harpys summoned on ’Sueño’, it all leaves us in no doubt that Arca is near the apex of her game here.

items.body:
Epic 16 hour François Bayle retrospective, an unparalleled document of the key C.20th electro-acoustic and concrète pioneer and director of the hugely influential GRM institution from 1966-1997, where he was instrumental in bringing the Acousmonium speaker array and INA-GRM label to life, among many important, enduring innovations

This 10 year reissue of ’50 Ans d’Acousmagique’ joins INA-GRM’s quintessential boxsets of Pierre Schaeffer, Pierre Henry, Parmegiani, Radigue, and Xenakis in a rare, stellar microcosm of works by twentieth century groundbreakers. At 16 hrs long, and including 228 tracks, it offers a comprehensive overview of François Bayle’s unfathomable catalogue of work between 1972-2012. During this time Bayle was pivotal in altering perceptions of music’s materiality and purpose at the most fundamental and philosophic levels through his work in developing the Acousmonium diffusion system - an “orchestra of loudspeakers” which has become key to the GRM’s facilities in Paris - as well as supporting technological developments (Syter, GRM Tools, Midi Formers, Acousmographe) which are vital to his own remarkable compositions, and his endeavours organising radio broadcasts and events. 

Deeply informing and paralleling the history of recorded electronic music during its formative golden years, Bayle’s recordings render an embarrassment of riches for the discerning and explorative listener and historians of vanguard C.20th music. Between the flighty electro-acoustic staging of his avian dreams on ’72’s ‘Trois Rêves D'oiseau’ to the sensually lathered cosmic delirium of 1978-80’s ‘Erosphère’ works, to his beguiling latter tributes to his tutors at the Paris Conservatoire and Darmstadt summer courses, Messiaen and Stockhausen; the overwhelming scope of Bayle’s work, and thus the boxset, is brought into clearer focus by its chronological sequencing, offering a logical pathway thru his incredible projections of imagination.

It bears reflection that figures such as François Bayle created, and then opened, doors of perception for music in the past century that have come to mirror and shape the soundsphere we now inhabit. His innovations in sound spatialisation and the embrace of an acoustic unknown, or acousmagique, underline some of the most fascinating expressions of pathos thru art in our lifetimes, and this boxset is more than enough to send heads reeling into deep time for eons to come.

Big room fuel by Tom & Ed Russell’s Overmono, condensing and refining the energy of their ‘Pure Devotion’ megadome events into Pavlovian cues for obedient ravers. OK no bush-beating, it’s torrid stuff that epitomises the schism of music for clubs, dancing, vs corporate-sponsored stages, PR, playlists...

“Sharing a name with the beloved series of live events they launched in 2024, Pure Devotion is Overmono’s most ambitious project to date. It’s the sound of beautiful imperfections, machine malfunctions and happy accidents, harnessed by the unflinching confidence that Overmono - aka brothers Tom and Ed Russell - have gained through years at the vanguard of underground electronic music, and subsequent breakthrough as one of the defining dance music acts of the decade.

Across the 11 tracks, Overmono have pushed their recording process into bold new territories, adopting experimental production techniques that involve synthesisers from the 70s and 80s, an antiquated train announcement speaker, and literally baking a crash cymbal in the oven. There’s a powerful sense of intention and physicality embedded in every choice, which extends to the emotive vocal features from revered British poet John Joseph Holt, close collaborator Kindora, and Paul Institute’s Ruthven It’s an album that chooses emotion over desensitisation. Craft over efficiency. It's a labour of love. Pure Devotion.

What started as a radical reimagining of Overmono’s live show in 2024 evolved into a phenomenon - from headlining Glastonbury’s West Holts to selling out London’s Alexandra Palace and curating Manchester’s Warehouse Project. As Pure Devotion grew onstage in front of tens of thousands of people, its core ideas deepened and crystallised via isolated writing and recordings retreats to Spain and Iceland with nothing but two synths and an FX unit, channeling the momentum into the most life-affirming and groundbreaking music of their career.”

Breezy new age house by an Antipodean artist with illustrious credits beside Michal Hutchence, Bono, Jamiroquai since the ‘80s, evened out with Kuniyuki and 451 remixes...

"Originally emerging from Melbourne’s post-punk and new wave underground in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Gus Till has spent more than four decades navigating a remarkably diverse musical path. From early electronic experimentation with Third Eye alongside Ollie Olsen, through a pivotal role in the formative years of the global psy-trance movement and collaborations with artists including Michael Hutchence, System 7, Manu Dibango, Todd Terry and Bim Sherman, Till’s work has consistently resisted easy categorisation, moving fluidly between ambient music, downtempo, house, trance and psychedelic electronica.

First released on Japan’s Dakini Records in 2006, ‘Rainsong’ captures many of these threads in a single expansive composition. Built around a pulsating bassline, layered live percussion and soaring vocal elements, the track sits comfortably between the dancefloor and more immersive listening environments. Unfolding patiently across nearly thirteen minutes, it combines hypnotic rhythmic momentum with a rich sense of atmosphere and musicality.

For the B-side, Kuniyuki Takahashi offers a distinct reinterpretation of the original. His remix gradually unfolds from a patient introduction into a deep and richly textured exploration of the track’s core themes. Subtle spatial processing, nuanced arrangement shifts and his unmistakable sense of atmosphere transform the source material while preserving its emotional core."

items.body:
Steve Rachmad's "Light And Time" via Dekmantel.

"Making a bold change of direction as he toasts 45 years working in electronic music, Steve Rachmad dials up the symphonic dimension of his musical practice for Light and Time — a widescreen trip to techno's outer reaches. As one of the true originators of Dutch dance music, Rachmad brings a wealth of experience to his first album for Dekmantel even as he adopts new production methods to create his most ambient body of work to date.

A strong melodic sensibility runs through all of Rachmad's work. His 1995 album The Secret Life Of Machines under his Sterac alias remains a landmark of lush, emotionally charged, deep-diving techno, while classic workouts like 'Helix' and 'Gnosis' (as Parallel 9) foregrounded powerful synth lines. Up until the upheaval of COVID, Rachmad's studio practice had been squarely focused on synths and drum machines, but when (along with the rest of the world) he was stuck at home reevaluating his situation, he found himself exploring the world of film scoring.

Experimenting with Native Instruments' sampling software Kontakt, Rachmad taught himself how to arrange and layer orchestral instrumentation. Having rarely used sampling in his music before, the distinct fluctuations of recorded orchestral players opened up a new dimension that has become the foundation of Light and Time, the first of many albums Rachmad has ready to go in a more downtempo, home-listening vein.

Throughout Light and Time, harmonious passages take centre stage as Rachmad audibly stretches out. At times the orchestral samples arrive in a pure, organic form, while elsewhere they merge and mutate into synthesised elements. His techno legacy manifests throughout, in abstract form. In lieu of strident beats, we're offered fractal, scratchy rhythms guiding uniquely shaped noise and natural sounding percussion with a human lilt. These fluctuations are no accident — they're a result of Rachmad playing much more of the album by hand after years in thrall to the precise machine pulse of arpeggios and sequences.

The album never feels restricted by one dogmatic approach. At times, Rachmad's embrace of moody soundtrack composition fills the whole picture, as on haunting string piece 'The Field Of Reality'. Elsewhere he dips into low-slung electro soul for 'Invisible Warriors Of Light' while 'Cosmic Memories' revels in alien synthesis with a dramatic bite. 'Encrypted Instructions' tweaks and processes string samples through angular prisms to close the album out with an experimental flourish.

Rachmad's long and winding history in electronic music naturally folds into these new modes of expression, and the end result is a sumptuous, many-sided album that showcases the hidden depths of a techno legend's musicality."

items.body:
Quietly unheimlich, slowcore dream-pop transformations of Western and Japanese kids’ music by a nascent Osaka duo for Em Records...weird and wonderful like some lost hookup between Tennoscoats, Colleen and Félicia Atkinson...

"The terms “nursery rhymes” and “children’s songs” may give rise to visions of idyllic innocence and the charms of childhood, but Play Nursery Rhymes and Children's Songs brings forth quite different aural imagery: this is an eerie and unsettling sonic picture book which hints at the darkness and mystery which form the hidden heart of many traditional songs and rhymes. The length of the songs provides a hint: each piece delves deeply into the latent uncanniness of the music, with superficial innocence gradually displaced as electric guitar, bass, field recordings and concrete sounds draw the listener into a chilly forest, while Tokiyo Ooto’s voice croons dark “lullabies for adults,” blending elements of folk, slowcore and dream pop.

The Tokiyo Ooto & Orhythmo duo formed in 2023, releasing their first album in 2024. This release updates two pieces from the first album, and also includes a traditional Japanese children’s song from Shiga Prefecture and a masterpiece for children by composer Yasushi Akutagawa. Both musicians are Osaka-based: Otoo is a guitarist and singer-songwriter who also works in band and solo contexts; Orhythmo is a bassist with hardcore punk roots who focuses on improvisation, drone, noise and ambient sound."

items.body:
Balmat alum Patricia Wolf flits to Ransom Note’s ambient tape series with a 45 min session of carefully pruned synth wooze and new age whims evoking private press cassettes via early ‘90s garden centres.

"‘Yarrow’ is a bouquet of new music by Portland, Oregon-based musician and field recordist Patricia Wolf, marking the label’s ninth release and the third of Season Two. The works are her reflections on the life cycle of plants and their dynamic ecological relationships.

Wolf created the album in response to her artist residency at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, Colorado, as part of the Art-Science Exchange Project in the summer of 2024. She worked closely with ecologists Dr Paul CaraDonna, Dr Amy Iler, Dr Jane Ogilvie, Dr Nickolas Waser, Dr Mary Price, and Dr Will Petry, spending weeks engaged in long-term research on plants, pollinators, and their interactions as the climate changes. 

Each track on Yarrow looks at a different part of a plant’s life. The songs touch on the conditions that plants need to grow, the quiet life of roots, how flowers attract pollinators, and the strength of seeds. The first single, 'Inflorescence', the scientific name for the floral display that a plant makes in an effort to reproduce, captures this event in song. The music slowly builds layers, reflecting the album’s overall feel. The album ends with the majestic Boards of Canada-esque 'Adapted for Extreme Conditions', and the entire b-side features Patricia’s field recordings from around Gothic, Colorado, and a guided meditation by Dr Paul CaraDonna, whose research inspired the project, inviting listeners to tune into the sounds and activities of the ecosystem."
